8474.9 in, §66, the mean of the four sides of the raised square of rock, mean difference 1.5 in. §65 explains the square: the builders cut the rock higher under the casing than under the pavement, so the raised square outlives the casing and marks the original extent of the Pyramid. Petrie fixed twelve points on it and adopted the four corners as probably the most accurately executed; the other fixed points differ from the adopted square by .9 in on average, and no probable error is stated. §66 checks the square against the lowest corners of the casing still standing high on the Pyramid, observed in the triangulation: they lie + 1.7, + .6, + .6 and + .3 in outside the diagonals of the raised square, mean + .7 in, so the casing planes were skewed round by + 1′40″ going up.

53°10′ ± 4′, §67, Petrie’s best statement of the angle of slope. The direct goniometer and level measures on the granite in situ give 53°12′ ± 2′, and 53°2′ from a plumb line, the block having been slightly shifted; 24 blocks of granite and limestone lying around the Pyramid give 53°14′ ± 5′, on the assumption that their courses were horizontal.

4153.6 in, §80, the mean of the E., S. and W. sides, mean difference 3.0 in. The N. end of the W. side could not be reached after several attempts, so §80 states no length for the N. side and no azimuth for the W. one, and the mean is of three sides only. Petrie’s sides do not differ by direction the way Lehner’s tabulated 102.2 by 104.6 m do: his three measured sides span 8.6 in, about 0.2 m. §80 adds three check points, which fall .8, 4.3 and .9 in outside the adopted square. §80 reduces the data that lie on higher levels to the adopted base level by the angle 51°0′. §79 puts that level one mean granite course, 40.3 ± 1.5 in, below the first joint, the casing having been left in the rough and its true foot nowhere visible. 51°0′ ± 10′, §81, Petrie’s best conclusion from the measured angles, which are divergent: 7 measures on finished granite in situ give 50°57′ ± 28″, the 1st and 4th courses in situ at the S.S.W. 50°42′ ± 7″, 6 shifted blocks of granite 51°0′ ± 9″, and 9 pieces of limestone casing brought to England 51°58′ ± 15″. §81 and §82 offer 51°10′30″ ± 1′20″ instead, from the granite casing ceasing at one quarter of the height, and say it might well be adopted.

2564 ± 15 in, §81, the height following from the mean base of §80 and the adopted angle 51°0′ ± 10′. §82 gives 2580.8 ± 2.0 in instead, four times the 645.2 in at which the granite casing ceases, which Petrie argues is one quarter of the height; that is 65.55 m against the 65.13 m stored here. Petrie measured no height directly.

+ 14′3″, §80, the mean of the three sides whose azimuth could be measured: N. + 16′48″, E. + 12′23″, S. + 12′57″. Positive is east of north, so the Third Pyramid is turned the opposite way from the First and the Second, which lie about 4′ to 5′ west of north. §80 states no probable error, only a mean difference of 1′50″, and sigma is that. §93 sets the Third Pyramid aside as too inferior in work to enter the determination of the pole, and §80 notes that a different base level would change none of these azimuths.
Lehner gives 72.55 m in places; verify.

29°58′31″ N, the commonly cited position of the monument. Sigma of 0.0005°, about 55 m, covers the spread between citations and the fact that no point of the statue is named. Unverified placeholder; replace with an ARCE or GPMP position.

31°08′16″ E, the commonly cited position of the monument. Sigma of 0.0005°, about 48 m at this latitude. Unverified placeholder. No azimuth for the Sphinx's own east-west axis is entered: none of the sources in data/sources.json states one here, so claim C5 takes due east from the plan's wording and says so.

13931.6 in, §92, N column of the table of relative positions (centre of the First to centre of the Second Pyramid); 353.86 m at 0.0254 m/inch. Petrie heads the columns N and E, but the Second Pyramid lies south and west of the First, so this is stored as a southward offset. His parallels are inclined −5′ to true north, the mean azimuth of the First and Second Pyramids, whereas this repo's frame is east-north-up on true north; at this distance 5′ is a cross-track shift of 0.51 m. Petrie's figure is kept unrotated, and he states no error for these distances, so sigma is that shift rounded up.

645.2 in, §82, the level at which the granite casing ceases, the top of the 16th course in the N.E. course table reduced to the adopted base level: “The granite is here marked as ceasing at 645.2, i.e., including the lower 16 courses.” Petrie’s evidence is that the highest remaining fragments of granite, the back ends of casing stones, stand at the same level on every side; that the 17th course is thicker than any other course of the whole Pyramid, as if a fresh start were made there, and is followed by one thinner than any below it; and that Diodorus has the casing of black stone to the 15th course. He remarks that the granite just covered one quarter of the height, and takes 645.2 × 4 = 2580.8 ± 2 as a determination of the original height. Sigma is his “± .5 (?) for uncertainty of paving”. Petrie also notes, §79, that the granite was left undressed over most of the faces.
“including the lower 16 courses”, §82, the courses of the N.E. table that the granite casing covers, its top at 645.2 in. See g3.casing.granite.height for Petrie’s three reasons.

41.52 ± .05 in, §68: “The lowest course of casing was of granite, and is 41.52 ± .05 high, vertically, from the top to the base of its slope, and its vertical face below that 11 high, as measured at the S.W.” §65 says the lowest two courses of the casing are of granite, with Petrie’s own footnote: “I have seen but one course; Vyse reports finding two courses.” Only the course Petrie measured is entered; if Vyse is right the granite reaches the top of the second course, which the S.W. column of the §68 course table puts at 86.5 in. The upper part was cased in Mokattam limestone, §68.
